title: The way you say it
subtitle: mumble, shriek, bicker, wind someone up, tongue-tied
summary: Describe exactly how something was said - from mumbling and murmuring to yelling and roaring - and name the styles of talk, from bickering and whingeing to buttering someone up.

lesson.heading: Speaking quietly
lesson.text: **Mumble** and **mutter** are both usually negative. **Murmur** can be more positive, and the phrase **without a murmur** means without any protest, complaint or comment.

examples.text: Stop **mumbling**! I can't hear what you're saying.
He was **muttering** something under his breath - probably complaining, as usual.
They **murmured** their approval when he told them the plan.
They accepted it all **without a murmur**. I was surprised; normally they argue about everything.

lesson.heading: Speaking loudly
lesson.text: To **raise your voice** is simply to speak louder - but it can also be an accusation. **Shout**, **yell**, **scream**, **roar** and **shriek** are all followed by **at**.

examples.text: You'll have to **raise your voice** a bit. She's a little hard of hearing.
Don't you **raise your voice at** me!
examples.note: = do not speak in that loud, angry tone

lesson.heading: Choosing the right loud verb
rows: yell
urgency, anger or frustration; also used when there is a lot of surrounding noise
'Stay where you are!' he yelled above the noise of the traffic.
shriek
loud and very high-pitched; positive or negative
'Oh, wow! That's fantastic!' she shrieked.
roar
very loud but deeper-pitched, like a lion; positive or negative
The crowd roared as he kicked the ball into the back of the net.
scream
loud, high and usually alarmed or furious
She screamed at him to get out of the house.

lesson.heading: Styles of conversation
rows: nag (at)
criticise faults or duties not done
Tom and Lily are always nagging each other.
bicker (synonym: squabble)
argue in an irritated way, usually about something petty
Stop bickering over who sits by the window, you two!
slag off
criticise in an insulting way; very informal
They spent all evening slagging off their colleagues.
whine and whinge
complain in an annoying way; informal and negative
Jessie is always whining and whingeing.
chat away
light, non-serious talk; away emphasises that it goes on and on
He's been chatting away on the phone all morning.
gossip
talk about people, rumours and their private affairs
We always gossip about work when we go out together.

lesson.heading: Teasing, flattering and overstating
lesson.text: To **wind someone up** is to tease or fool them; the noun is **a wind-up**, often **a complete wind-up**. To **butter someone up** is to say nice things because you want something from them. To **exaggerate** is to make something seem greater than it really is (noun: **exaggeration**), and to **generalise** is to make general statements (noun: **generalisation**).

examples.text: It took him a long time to realise they were **winding him up**.
I realised she was **buttering me up**.
Rick tends to **exaggerate** his problems, so don't take him too literally.
Meg is inclined to **generalise** on the basis of her very limited experience.

lesson.heading: Speech and articulation problems
rows: She speaks with a lisp. She says 'thing' instead of 'sing'.
difficulty in making an 's' sound, and making a 'th' sound instead
He hates speaking in front of people because he's got a really bad stammer.
speaking with abnormal pauses and repetitions
'I want to t-t-t-tell you something,' she stuttered nervously.
repeating sounds at the beginning of words
He was slurring his words because he had drunk far too much alcohol.
his words had a slow, lazy sound, difficult to understand
I want to tell her I love her, but I get tongue-tied.
cannot say what I want to say because of nerves - an emotional rather than physical problem

lesson.text: A shriek goes up in pitch, a roar goes down - think of a child on a rollercoaster versus a lion.

exercises.prompt: Which verb means 'to argue in an irritated manner about something petty'?
exercises.explanation: Bicker (synonym: squabble) is to argue in an irritated way, usually about something trivial.

exercises.prompt: How is roar different from shriek?
options: Roar is deeper, like a lion; shriek is very high-pitched.
Roar is very high-pitched; shriek is deeper.
Roar is quiet; shriek is loud.
Roar is always positive; shriek is always negative.
exercises.explanation: Both are very loud, but roar suggests a deep, lion-like sound and shriek a very high-pitched one.

exercises.prompt: They accepted it all without a ___ . I was surprised; normally they argue about everything.
exercises.explanation: Without a murmur means without any protest, complaint or comment.

exercises.prompt: 'I want to c-c-c-come with you,' she ___ nervously.
exercises.explanation: To stutter or stammer is to repeat sounds and speak with abnormal pauses.

exercises.prompt: Lara got ___ , perhaps because of the famous people present, and didn't say a word all evening.
exercises.explanation: To be tongue-tied is to be unable to say what you want because of nerves.

exercises.prompt: I wish you'd speak up and stop ___ . I can't hear a word you're saying.
exercises.hint: (-ing form; speaking too quietly and unclearly)
exercises.explanation: Mumble and mutter both describe speaking quietly and indistinctly, and both are negative.

exercises.prompt: I had to ___ at him to be heard, the noise of the plane was so loud.
exercises.explanation: Yell often conveys urgency and is used when there is a lot of surrounding noise.
Murmur is the quiet verb that can be positive.

exercises.prompt: The drugs had made her speech very incoherent. She was ___ all her words.
exercises.explanation: If you slur your words, they have a slow, lazy sound and are difficult to understand.

exercises.prompt: She speaks with a ___ - she says 'whithper' instead of 'whisper'.
exercises.explanation: A lisp is difficulty in making an 's' sound, so that it comes out as 'th'.

exercises.prompt: I know Ben is a little strange but you can't ___ about all Canadians just because of him.
exercises.explanation: To generalise is to make general statements about something; the noun is generalisation.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word: 'They're always ___ and whingeing about everything.'
exercises.explanation: To whine and whinge is to complain in an annoying way.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct phrase: 'Do you think Peggy was trying to ___ me up? She was saying all those nice things about me.'
exercises.explanation: To butter someone up is to say nice things because you want something from them.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word: 'You're always ___ me! Just leave me alone and let me watch TV!'
exercises.explanation: To nag someone is to criticise their faults or the things they have not done.

exercises.statement: If someone is winding you up, they are teasing or fooling you.
exercises.explanation: Correct - the noun is a wind-up, often a complete wind-up.
